newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil antitrust moves seen scaring off foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Brazil antitrust moves seen scaring off foreigners.

text.p: A Brazilian anti-trust watchdog agency, once considered a marginal player in the corporate world, flexed its muscles this month by squashing two major U.S. investments in a move that could discourage foreign investment, financial analysts said.

The rulings by Administrative Economic Defense Council (Cade) dissolving partnerships involving Miller Brewing Company and Anheuser-Busch could dampen overseas investor interest and brake the largely foreign-fueled acceleration of mergers and acquisitions in Brazil, they said.
"Nobody expected that decision and, if it becomes the rule, it may end up being an obstacle to new deals," said Raul Beer, director at Price Waterhouse consulting firm.

A Price recent study showed mergers and acquisitions jumped 19 percent to 387 in 1996, from 325 the prior year, specially in the beverage, food, financial, autoparts, computer, chemical and petrochemical sectors.
Capital from abroad was behind 50 percent of acquisitions and took part in 78 percent of the joint-ventures, it said.
Cade's latest strike came last week when in a preliminary ruling it ordered that local Cia. Antarctica Paulista dissolve a venture with Anheuser-Busch, the world's largest brewer, within two years.

The decision came on the heels of a Cade's order two weeks ago to also undo within 24 months the two-year-old joint venture between South America's largest brewer Brahma and U.S. giant Miller, a unit of Philip Morris Cos .
Analysts said that preventing foreigners from joining forces with local firms does not necessarily mean they will invest on their own in Brazil.

"The prohibition to enter the Brazilian market through associations with local players cannot guarantee foreign competitors will invest directly in the country," said Caspian Securities Lilyanna Yang in a recent report.

Foreign direct investment is key for Brazil's management of its burgeoning current account deficit, which this year is expected to reach $35 billion. Over 40 percent of the current account gap has been financed by direct investment, which totalled $6.3 billion in the first five months.
The Cade found the 1995 Brahma-Miller venture impedes competition in the sector, saying Miller could have entered the Brazilian beer market on its own. That ruling is being appealed by Brahma.

As for the Antarctica-Anheuser case, five of the seven members of the council voted in favor of dissolving the deal but a final ruling was postponed until July 2. Brahma and Antarctica hold nearly 90 percent of the Brazilian beer market.
But the U.S. brewers were not the first U.S. companies to be obliged to change plans because of the antitrust action.

Last year, the Cade approved Colgate-Palmolive's acquisition of the Brazilian oral hygiene firm Anakol, producer of Kolynos toothpaste in the country. But Colgate was forced to suspend the sale of Kolynos brand in Brazil for four years, one of the three conditions set by Cade to give its green light to the purchase.

The role of antitrust agencies in the economy has gained another dimension in recent years as Brazil's economic stability and privatization drive led to a boom in mergers and buyouts and concentration in some sectors.

The Cade rulings came amid a decision by another antitrust body to begin a probe into the steel, pharmaceutical and aluminum sectors to investigate allegations of price-setting and excessive price increases.

The Justice Ministry's Economic Law department ordered three major local steelmakers to suspend their planned hike in steel prices on allegations that it formed a cartel. It also determined that Hoescht Marion Roussell, a unit of pharmaceutical group Hoescht AG, should cut drug prices.
The Cade votes against the breweries brought sharp criticism from Cade's own president Gesner de Oliveira, who accused fellow members of "xenophobia."
"A country like Brazil, which needs investments, has to avoid any kind of tutelage regarding how that investment comes in," Oliveira was quoted by local newspapers as saying.
Lucia Helena Salgado e Silva, the Cade member who proposed the dissolution of the brewery ventures in two years, dismissed fears that foreign investors will shun Brazil because of the rulings.

"It is pure paranoia to think that those two decisions could paralyse Brazil's foreign investment wave," she told Folha de Sao Paulo daily in an interview. "Capital does not move emotionally. It moves on its interests."
Salgado e Silva insisted the brewery deals were isolated cases.

"We analysed about 32 cases in the last year, a large part of which involved acquisitions of Brazilian firms by foreigners, and we approved all of them," she said. "The Cade expressed no prejudice or censorship."
((--Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 2485412))
